However, if the underlying pays dividends, then early exercise may be optimal, and there is no closed-form analytical solution in general; instead, there are approximations (like Barone-Adesi and Whaley, Bjerksund and Stensland) or numerical methods. This is a well-known result proved by Merton (1973). Therefore, the analytical solution is the Black-Scholes formula. However, if dividends are present (continuous dividend yield q > 0), then early exercise may be optimal just before the ex-dividend date. For continuous dividend yield, there is still no simple closed-form solution for the American call, but there are analytical approximations. Some sources might refer to the "analytical solution" as the solution to the free-boundary problem, which can be expressed in terms of an integral equation (like the Kim integral equation) but that is not a closed-form formula. Alternatively, there is the Roll-Geske-Whaley model for a single discrete dividend, which provides a closed-form solution involving bivariate normal distributions. But that is for discrete dividends. This answer reflects the consensus in quantitative finance: **Only the non-dividend case has a simple analytical solution.** For dividend-paying assets, "analytical solution" refers either to specialized closed-forms (single dividend) or high-accuracy approximations—not a universal formula. Always verify dividend assumptions before selecting a pricing method.
